paragraph: CALLED AN APOSTLE WITH PAUL (ACTS 14:14) · CALLED IN ACTS 11

blocks.text: CALLED AN APOSTLE WITH PAUL (ACTS 14:14) · CALLED IN ACTS 11
Barnabas. The Levite from Cyprus who vouched for Saul, taught with him at Antioch, and went out with him on the first journey.
ALSO CALLED
Joses (KJV, Acts 4:36); Joseph in the Revised Version
FROM
“A Levite, and of the country of Cyprus” (Acts 4:36); Acts first finds him in the Jerusalem church.
TRADE
Scripture gives him no trade.
FAMILY
A Levite by tribe.
WRITINGS
Hebrews: Tertullian named Barnabas as its writer; the letter names none (see the question below and the Hebrews page)
BACKGROUND
Home, trade and family
FROM
TRADE
FAMILY
A Levite by tribe. Acts 4:36

From the textMark is “sister's son to Barnabas” in the KJV (Colossians 4:10). The Greek word, anepsios, is rendered “cousin” in the Revised Version (1881); Jacobs (ISBE, 1915) notes it is used in Numbers 36:11 for the sons of a father's brothers. Colossians 4:10

Scholars' viewOur person data makes Barnabas the brother of Mary, the mother of John Mark. That rests on the KJV's “sister's son”; with “cousin” the link is less close, and Scripture does not say how they were related. Colossians 4:10 Acts 12:12 [22]
THE CALLING
Called, as 2 accounts tell it
“they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch.”
Acts 11:22 (KJV) →
WHERE HE WENT
Acts and after
Dashed pins are places known only from later tradition, not from Scripture.
Cyprus · His home country; first stop of the first journey; where he sailed with Mark. Acts 4:36 Acts 13:4 +1 more
Jerusalem · Where he sold his land, brought Saul to the apostles, and came for the council. Acts 4:37 Acts 9:26–27 +3 more
Antioch (Syria) · Where he and Saul taught for a whole year, and from where they were sent out. Acts 11:22–26 Acts 13:1–3 +2 more
Tarsus · Where he went to find Saul. Acts 11:25
Seleucia · The port they sailed from. Acts 13:4
Salamis · First preaching on Cyprus, in the synagogues. Acts 13:5
Paphos · Sergius Paulus believed; Elymas was struck blind. Acts 13:6–12
Perga · Where John Mark left them; they preached there on the way back. Acts 13:13 Acts 14:25
Antioch in Pisidia · “We turn to the Gentiles”; expelled from the district. Acts 13:14 Acts 13:50 +1 more
Iconium · A long stay, then flight from a plot to stone them. Acts 13:51 Acts 14:1–6
Lystra · Hailed as Jupiter. Acts 14:6–20
Derbe · Taught many before turning back. Acts 14:20–21
Attalia · The port of the return voyage. Acts 14:25–26
Salamis (his death, in tradition) · tradition · The Acts of Barnabas (written before 478) has him burned to death here.
IN ACTS AND THE LETTERS
He sold land he owned and laid the money at the apostles' feet. Acts 4:36–37
When the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of the converted Saul, Barnabas “took him, and brought him to the apostles” and told how he had seen the Lord and preached boldly at Damascus. Acts 9:26–28
At Antioch he went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him back; for a whole year they taught there, “And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.” Acts 11:25–26
He and Saul carried the Antioch church's famine relief to the elders in Judaea, and came back with John Mark. Acts 11:29–30 Acts 12:25
On the first journey they preached at Salamis and crossed Cyprus to Paphos, where the deputy Sergius Paulus “called for Barnabas and Saul” and believed. Acts 13:4–12
At Antioch in Pisidia “Paul and Barnabas waxed bold”: “lo, we turn to the Gentiles”; they were expelled and went on to Iconium. Acts 13:44–51
At Lystra the crowd “called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius”; the two tore their clothes and stopped the sacrifice. After Paul was stoned, he left with Barnabas for Derbe. Acts 14:8–20
Returning, they ordained elders in every church and told the church at Antioch how God “had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles”. Acts 14:21–28

From the textUntil Paphos Acts says “Barnabas and Saul” (11:30; 12:25; 13:2, 7); from there it mostly says “Paul and Barnabas” (13:43, 46, 50; 15:2, 22, 35), though “Barnabas and Paul” comes back at Lystra and in Jerusalem (14:14; 15:12, 25). Acts 11:30 Acts 12:25 Acts 13:2 Acts 13:7 Acts 13:43 Acts 13:46 +7 more

Over circumcision, he and Paul had “no small dissension” with men from Judaea and went up to Jerusalem; at the council the multitude “gave audience to Barnabas and Paul”, and the letter called them “our beloved Barnabas and Paul, Men that have hazarded their lives”. Acts 15:1–4 Acts 15:12 Acts 15:25–26
Paul writes that he went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and that James, Cephas and John gave “to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship”. Galatians 2:1 Galatians 2:9
At Antioch, when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles, “Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation”. Galatians 2:13

Barnabas wanted to take John Mark on a second journey; Paul refused, because Mark had left them in Pamphylia. “The contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder”; Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus. Acts 15:36–39

From the textActs does not mention him again after Acts 15:39. Paul still names him in 1 Corinthians 9:6, and in Colossians 4:10 tells the church to receive Mark, “sister's son to Barnabas”. Acts 15:39 1 Corinthians 9:6 Colossians 4:10
COMPANIONS
Who was with him
Each line joins him to someone Scripture places beside him.

Paul (Saul) He vouched for Saul in Jerusalem, brought him to Antioch, and worked with him through the first journey and the council, until they parted over Mark. Acts 9:27 Acts 11:25–26 Acts 13:2 Acts 15:39
John Mark His relative (Colossians 4:10); taken to Antioch and on the first journey, and later to Cyprus. Acts 12:25 Acts 13:5 Acts 15:37–39 Colossians 4:10
Simeon called Niger A prophet or teacher with him at Antioch. Acts 13:1
Lucius of Cyrene A prophet or teacher with him at Antioch. Acts 13:1
Manaen A prophet or teacher with him at Antioch, “brought up with Herod the tetrarch”. Acts 13:1
Judas Barsabas Sent with Barnabas and Paul to carry the council's letter to Antioch. Acts 15:22 Acts 15:27
Silas Sent with them to Antioch; Paul later chose Silas when he and Barnabas parted. Acts 15:22 Acts 15:40
Titus Went up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas. Galatians 2:1
Sergius Paulus The deputy of Cyprus who called for Barnabas and Saul and believed. Acts 13:7 Acts 13:12
Peter (Cephas) Gave him and Paul the right hand of fellowship; at Antioch Barnabas followed Peter's withdrawal from the Gentiles. Galatians 2:9 Galatians 2:13
HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
From the textScripture does not record his death. Acts last shows him sailing to Cyprus with Mark (Acts 15:39). Acts 15:39
TRADITION SAYS

Barnabas is seized in the synagogue at Salamis at the urging of Bar-jesus, dragged out of the city with a rope round his neck, and burned; Mark hides the ashes in a cave and sails to Alexandria. The work is told in Mark's name.[6] Who says so: The Journeyings and Martyrdom of St. Barnabas the Apostle (the Acts of Barnabas), written before AD 478, says the introduction in the Ante-Nicene Fathers; McGiffert dates it once to the 5th century and once to the 3rd
In 478, it is said, the body of Barnabas was found in Cyprus.[6] Who says so: Reported in the introduction to the apocryphal Acts, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8 (1886), AD 478

A list of the Seventy printed among the doubtful works of Hippolytus names “Barnabas, bishop of Milan”. McGiffert calls the silence of Ambrose, bishop of Milan in the 4th century, “a sufficient proof of its groundlessness”.[11][2] Who says so: “On the Seventy Apostles”, attributed to Hippolytus, date unknown; its editor calls it “Probably spurious, but yet antique”
WRITINGS
Writings tied to him
LETTERS
Hebrews: Tertullian named Barnabas as its writer; the letter names none (see the question below and the Hebrews page)
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
Yes
Tertullian, On Modesty 20 (not earlier than AD 208); in modern times Grau and Zahn, as reported by Jacobs (ISBE, 1915)
Tertullian quotes Hebrews 6 from “an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas”, calling him “a man sufficiently accredited by God”. Hebrews 6:4–6 [10][22]
Not settled: one of several names
Jerome (392), who gives Barnabas “according to Tertullian” beside Luke and Clement; Fenlon (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907), who thinks Tertullian's credit “probably” false

Jerome reports that the letter is not counted Paul's “on account of its difference from the others in style and language”, and lists the other names offered. The full views are on the Hebrews page.[3][18]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 10
Acts 4 Acts 9 Acts 11 Acts 12 Acts 13 Acts 14 Acts 15 1 Corinthians 9 Galatians 2 Colossians 4
PASSAGES · 9
Acts 4:36–37 Acts 9:26–30 Acts 11:19–30 Acts 12:25 Acts 13:1–14:28 Acts 15:1–41 1 Corinthians 9:6 Galatians 2:1–14 Colossians 4:10
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture does not say when or how Barnabas came to believe, or where the land he sold lay.
Scripture does not say whether he and Paul were reconciled after Acts 15, though Paul names him without blame in 1 Corinthians 9:6.
Scripture does not tell how or when he died.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON
His name was Joses (Joseph in other Greek texts); the apostles “surnamed” him Barnabas, “which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation”. Acts 4:36
From the textThe Revised Version (1881) renders the same words “Son of exhortation”; the Greek word, paraklēsis, carries both senses. Acts 4:36

Scholars' viewHow the name itself means this is debated: Jacobs (ISBE, 1915) derives it from bar, “son”, and a Hebrew word for prophecy, and reports Deissmann's suggestion that it meant “son of Nebo”.[22]
Luke calls him “a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith”, and with Paul one of “the apostles” at Lystra. Acts 11:24 Acts 14:4 Acts 14:14

Scholars' viewLightfoot (1890) holds that “the apostleship of Barnabas is beyond question”, since Luke records his sending at the same time and in the same way as Paul's (Acts 13:2-3). He was not one of the Twelve. Acts 13:2–3 [13]

Early church · Clement of Alexandria (trans. William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2), 1885Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200) calls him one of the Seventy (Luke 10:1) and “a fellow-worker of Paul”; McGiffert notes the tradition can be traced “no further than Clement”.[9][1][2]
Scholars' viewLuther and Calvin took “the brother, whose praise is in the gospel” (2 Corinthians 8:18) to be Barnabas, as Jacobs (ISBE, 1915) reports. The verse names no one. 2 Corinthians 8:18 [22]
